extracted.intended_audience: writers, readers, and students interested in novel-writing and narrative craft
extracted.subtask_description: Summarising E.M. Forster's key 'aspects' of the novel as guidance for evaluating or writing novels, focusing on story, plot, character types, and authorial technique. Notes highlight what makes novels work emotionally and structurally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronology is irrelevant / universality of aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster proposes that chronology is irrelevant in literature; novelists from all periods share underlying 'aspects of the novel' and can be considered together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose is to avoid focusing on trends/styles of particular periods and instead look for commonalities shared by novels across time and place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive story (sequence of events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'primitive' aspect: the story as a sequence—'and then this happened, and then that happened.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All novels should have a basic story at the centre to get and keep the reader's attention, though a good novel must have more than this simple chronological sequence. Example: cavemen telling stories around the fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: People/character as inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel characters differ from real people because the novelist can show their inner life, giving readers knowledge and a sense of certainty about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interior access provides solace and makes humans seem more understandable; fictional characters tend to be more sensitive and attention is often given to love rather than everyday facts (birth, food, sleep, death). The novelist's choice whether to show inner life affects how well we 'know' characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat vs round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters can be flat (types/caricatures, summable in a phrase) or round (complex, capable of development).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat characters have one function and perform it consistently; they can be effective for limited or comic roles (most of Dickens’s characters are cited as flats). Tragic figures generally must be round. Forster's test: a flat character is one that never surprises convincingly; if it never surprises it is flat, and if it does not convince it is 'a flat pretending to be round.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial self-consciousness / showing method is harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers who betray too much interest in their own method or 'draw readers into his confidence' by showing how the novel works weaken the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such self-consciousness prevents creation of character, summons readers to analyse the writer's mind, and causes 'a heavy drop in the emotional thermometer.' Forster implies this is an anti-pattern (metafictional ostentation undermines emotional engagement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: plot (causality) vs story (sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is a higher form than story because it deals with causality rather than mere sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: 'The king died and then the queen died' (story) vs 'The queen died...through grief at the death of the king' (plot). Plot requires the reader's memory and intelligence to fit facts from different parts of the novel and see how they connect by the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should be causal, coherent, and not misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: In a good plot, everything happens for a reason; it can contain mysteries but must not mislead the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot-maker expects readers to remember earlier details and to have loose ends tied up. The writer should avoid leaving loose ends or intentionally deceiving the reader about causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between character development and plot needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot and character can be at war, especially toward the denouement, when the writer attempts to pull the plot together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes characters may be corralled or made subservient to the plot (e.g., a character appears to change suddenly to serve a plot surprise). This is less faithful to character but may be justified if it produces a better plot surprise; the trade-off between fidelity to character and the demands of plot is a key judgement for the novelist.
